c.text:
Trigger: Before finalizing a chest-X-ray multiple-choice answer that chooses between left-base and right-base atelectasis/opacity when a phrase-grounding tool has returned a box for the proposed side.

Observable verification action: Do not treat phrase grounding as proof that the finding is present on that side; it only localizes the phrase you supplied. Require an independent report/expert statement that explicitly lateralizes the same finding to the same patient side, not merely “bibasilar opacities” and not an echo of your query. Convert any box coordinates to patient laterality—image right is patient left, image left is patient right—and check that this agrees with the explicit lateralized statement. If the only evidence is bilateral, ambiguous, or a query-echo box, do not finalize that side as confirmed; resolve with an independent reader or record the ambiguity. Then map the supported side and finding to the displayed option letter and text and check that both agree.

Case lesson: The original answer A matched option A’s text, so this was not an option-mapping error. The failure was evidence use: “mild bibasilar opacities” plus a phrase-grounding box for “left base pulmonary atelectasis” was treated as confirmation of left-base disease, even though the report was bilateral and the verifier itself noted right-base haziness. The verifier’s “CORRECT” label was not independent ground truth. The reference answer was B, so the terminal choice should have distinguished a confirmed lateralized finding from a merely localized query phrase.

Lesson: The terminal answer B, “elevated left diaphragm,” matches option B and the released reference, so this was not an option-mapping error. The evidence path was weaker: chest_xray_expert said Left, llava_med_qa said Right, and reflect warned that the projection/laterality marker had not been verified. The later chest_xray_expert “confirmation” embedded the suspected left/gastric-bubble reasoning, so it was a leading re-query rather than an independent check. The correct grade alone does not prove that resolution procedure works.

Narrow trigger: A chest X-ray multiple-choice item asks left versus right hemidiaphragm elevation when visual-tool outputs conflict or a reflection flags uncertain projection/laterality.

Observable verification action: Before finalizing, inspect the original/full image and explicitly confirm the view/projection and any side marker; obtain a neutral, non-leading side-identification check, or record the side as unresolved. Then map the supported finding text to the displayed option and verify that the letter and text agree. Do not treat a re-query that embeds the suspected side as confirmation, and do not use gastric-bubble left-side reasoning unless a lateral view is confirmed.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray question whose options differ by left vs right lung opacity, especially when the image has a laterality/projection label such as “LT LAT”/left lateral and a diagnostic tool call was proposed but no tool observation actually appears.

Verification action: Before choosing, require a returned interpretation that explicitly names the opacity and its side in the lung fields. Do not infer the side of the finding from “LT LAT” or “left lateral”; that describes the view/positioning, not the pathology, and on a lateral view the lungs overlap. If the tool-observation list is empty, treat the proposed tool call as unevaluated, not as evidence. Confirm the evidence addresses the same object and attribute as the question—opacity and left/right side. Then map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and check that its letter and text agree.

In this case, “A” matched “left lung opacity” by letter and text, so this was not an option-mapping error; it was an evidence/conclusion error. The final choice equated the LT LAT label with left lung opacity despite no executed expert observation. The released reference is B, right lung opacity.

Experience: In this case the terminal answer B (“surgical instruments in the left lung”) matched the released reference, so there was no option-letter/text mapping error. The caution is about the evidence chain: the expert tool was asked a side-leading question (“…in the left lung…?”) and returned only “Yes,” while the image was a lateral view and the ROI tool warned not to infer laterality from screen position. A correct grade does not make that one-sided confirmation sufficient proof of left-vs-right location.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray question whose options differ only by right vs left, especially after a lateral view or after a tool was asked only about one side and returned a simple yes/no.

Verification action: Before finalizing, check the original image for an explicit laterality marker such as “L” or “R,” or require an orthogonal/frontal or comparative left-vs-right observation; never infer side from crop screen position. Then map the supported side/text to the displayed option and verify that the letter and text agree. If no side marker or comparative evidence exists, do not treat the one-sided “Yes” as proof of laterality; state the limitation or seek orthogonal evidence.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray laterality answer after an expert tool gave a side, a verifier returned “CORRECT,” and the drafted rationale mentions which hemidiaphragm is higher/elevated.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the final answer, do a fixed cross-check. First, map the supported answer text to the displayed option and confirm the terminal letter and exact option text agree. Second, search the earlier draft/risk and tool observations for the same object and attribute—right vs left diaphragm elevation or relative height. If an earlier note says the opposite side/height from the final rationale, flag a conflict. Third, do not treat verifier “CORRECT” as evidence for the anatomical side or height; it checks the proposed answer, not the laterality claim. Re-check the original/crop only if patient side is marked or otherwise determinable, and do not infer patient laterality from screen position. If the conflict remains, either resolve it with a targeted observation or omit the unsupported rationale.

Case lesson: Here the terminal “B. elevated left diaphragm” matches option B and the released reference B, and chest_xray_expert said “Left,” so this was not an option-mapping error. But step 3’s risk note said the right hemidiaphragm was higher than the left and normal, while the final reason said the left was abnormally high relative to the right. The verify tool’s “CORRECT” did not resolve that contradiction; maira2_grounded_report did not address diaphragm elevation, and roi_crop warns that patient laterality cannot be inferred from screen position. A correct grade alone does not prove the final rationale is sound. The reusable safeguard is: at finalization, reconcile the option map, the terminal rationale, and the same-attribute evidence; verifier confirmation must not paper over an explicit contradiction.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer that names competing findings (for example, right versus left base atelectasis), and the rationale claims “multiple tools consistently” support the answer after one tool was given a candidate answer phrase for grounding.

Verification action: Before emitting the final option, classify each tool observation as independent presence evidence, location-only evidence for a phrase you supplied, or a different finding. Count only independent presence statements as confirmation. A phrase-grounding result for “left base pulmonary atelectasis” shows where that supplied phrase can be boxed; it does not by itself prove atelectasis is present. Check that the tool addressed the same object and attribute as the question—left versus right base and atelectasis versus effusion. If a direct report conflicts, such as a small left pleural effusion but no explicit atelectasis, do not describe the tools as uniformly agreeing. Then map the supported finding text to the displayed choice and verify that the letter and text match; here the reference was B, “left base pulmonary atelectasis,” so the option mapping was correct even though the “multiple tools consistently localize” rationale overstated the evidence.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice imaging answer whose options differ only by a discriminator that the available image or tool output does not directly establish—especially left-versus-right laterality on a lateral chest X-ray, or “surgical instruments” versus “metallic clips/wires”—and a verifier reports that the discriminating attribute is indeterminate or the tool results conflict.

Verification action: Before emitting the option letter, explicitly name the discriminating attribute required by the chosen option and check that the cited observation supports that exact attribute on the same object and image. Accept the option only if the evidence directly supports both the finding and the discriminator, such as “surgical instruments in the left lung”—not merely “metallic densities are present” plus an anatomical guess. If the evidence supports only nonspecific presence, a different object, or the verifier says laterality cannot be determined, do not infer the side from screen position, anterior location, or typical projection anatomy; mark the answer as unsupported or indeterminate and, if forced to choose, record the evidence gap and seek a frontal radiograph, CT, or report. Then map the supported answer text to the displayed choice and confirm that its letter and text agree.

In this case, the letter/text mapping was not the problem: “A. surgical instruments in the left lung” matched the reference. The problem was evidence finalization: the first CheXagent output said only “Yes,” LLaVA-Med said “No,” both verify calls warned that a lateral view cannot determine left versus right, and the verifier also noted that metallic clips/wires are not equivalent to surgical instruments. The final answer nonetheless converted partial, nonspecific evidence into a left-sided conclusion. The lesson is to treat a correct grade as insufficient proof of the procedure and to prevent side-specific finalization when laterality was never observed or verified.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray answer whose options differ only by laterality (e.g., elevated right vs left diaphragm) after a phrase-grounding call has been made.

Action: Before emitting the letter, identify the direct, non-echoed tool observation that answers the exact object and attribute—here chest_xray_expert answered “Left” to the right-vs-left hemidiaphragm question. Do not count xray_phrase_grounding as independent proof of the finding, because it was given “elevated left hemidiaphragm” and merely localized/repeated that phrase; also do not cite maira2’s left-base radiodensity as evidence of an elevated diaphragm. Then map the supported text to the displayed options and verify letter and text agree: B = “elevated left diaphragm,” matching the reference B. If the direct observation had said right, was absent, or conflicted, phrase grounding returning a left-sided box would not justify choosing left.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray finding after tool outputs show bilateral findings, mixed laterality, or a forced single-side choice (e.g., A “right pleural effusion” vs. B “left pleural effusion”).

Verification action: Before emitting the terminal answer, bind the supported side/finding to the displayed option map: read the final answer text, locate that exact text among the options, and confirm the letter and text agree. Then check that the cited side matches the evidence actually used. If the evidence says bilateral but the question forces one side, require the rationale to state the forced-choice basis—e.g., which side is dominant or more definitive—rather than silently turning bilateral disease into a solitary unilateral finding. Treat a letter/text mismatch as an option-mapping error; treat a side contradicted by the used evidence as a wrong conclusion. Do not rely on a verifier’s “CORRECT” label alone.

In this case, chest_xray_expert returned “Right,” maira2_grounded_report returned “Bilateral pleural effusion,” and verify said the right costophrenic angle was the more definitive/classic finding while the left could not be fully excluded. The terminal answer A. right pleural effusion matches the released reference A, so the reusable lesson is the final letter–text–side consistency check, plus explicit handling of bilateral evidence under a forced single-choice format.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality—e.g., “large right pleural effusion” vs. “large left pleural effusion”—and the rationale infers the side from a single lateral view, posterior layering, absence of a gastric bubble, or a laterality question that was only planned/asked but not answered.

Verification action: Before emitting the choice, inspect the executed tool observations and require at least one direct result that explicitly states the side of the pleural effusion—the same object and attribute as the question. Posterior layering opacity supports effusion, not right-vs-left laterality. An empty observation set, an unreturned chest_xray_expert call, or absence of a gastric bubble/ diaphragmatic cue cannot justify “left” over “right.” If direct evidence says right, map it to the option containing “large right pleural effusion”; if left, map to “large left pleural effusion”; then verify the displayed letter and text agree. In this case, B’s text matches option B (“large left pleural effusion”), so the option mapping was correct, but the side conclusion was unsupported and contradicted the reference A (“large right pleural effusion”). Treat that as a wrong conclusion from insufficient laterality evidence, not an option-mapping error.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest-X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ by laterality (e.g., right vs left lung opacity) after a direct expert/VQA call asked the same right-versus-left question.

Verification action: Use the tool reply only if it explicitly names the same finding and side on the same image; for example, “Left lung” directly supports “left lung opacity.” Do not count a phrase-grounding box, a report about a different finding, or an unqueried visual detail as independent confirmation. Map the supported finding-and-side text back to the displayed options and check that the emitted letter and text agree—here “left lung opacity” is option B, so B with that text is consistent. If the direct reply is absent, ambiguous, or addresses a different finding or side, do not finalize that side as confirmed.

Trigger: When a chest X-ray multiple-choice item asks left versus right pleural effusion, and the image is a single lateral view or the verifier warns that laterality cannot be reliably determined, especially after models disagree or are prompted to choose left/right.

Observable verification action: Before finalizing, check whether any tool result actually reports the same finding and side from a view or source capable of showing laterality, such as a frontal PA/AP view, decubitus view, or radiology report. Do not count left/right answers produced by asking a lateral-only image to lateralize as independent confirmation; treat “LT LAT” or “RT LAT” as a projection marker, not as evidence of the effusion side. If no valid laterality evidence remains, record the side as unresolved rather than taking a majority vote among lateral-view guesses. If the forced-choice format requires a side, state the explicit non-visual basis for that choice. Then map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and confirm the letter and text agree.

Lesson from this case: the terminal answer A “small left pleural effusion” matched option A, so this was not an option-mapping error; it was a wrong conclusion. The final rationale lost earlier cautions: chest_xray_expert initially said right, and verify twice warned that a lateral-only image cannot reliably lateralize the effusion. The left-side votes came from models asked to lateralize on that same inadequate view. The reusable check is to require view-appropriate evidence for laterality and avoid converting model-majority guesses into a definitive side.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray answer where the choices differ only by laterality—such as A “right indwelling catheter” versus B “left indwelling catheter”—and the image is a lateral view or the verifier/reflection says laterality is ambiguous or unconfirmed.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the letter, separate “finding is present” evidence from “side is confirmed” evidence. A tool response of only “Yes” confirms presence, not laterality. A single model saying “right” is not sufficient if the verifier explicitly says a lateral view superimposes right and left and laterality cannot be definitively determined. Do not describe the verifier’s warning as “no evidence contradicts” the side; that warning is a direct uncertainty/conflict. Require a non-leading independent side confirmation from a frontal projection, side marker, or radiology report; otherwise record the side as unresolved rather than choosing a side from one lateral-view model output. Then map the supported text to the displayed option and confirm that the letter and text agree.

In this case, the terminal letter/text mapping was internally consistent—A matched “right indwelling catheter”—but the conclusion was not supported: chest_xray_expert returned only “Yes,” llava_med_qa supplied “right,” and the verifier then stated laterality could not be confirmed on the lateral view. The released reference was B, “left indwelling catheter.” This was therefore not an option-mapping error; it was an evidence/laterality conclusion error. The reusable caution is to avoid converting ambiguous laterality into a confident side, and to require independent side evidence before finalizing.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality, such as elevated right versus left hemidiaphragm, and earlier visual tools have returned side-specific text.

Observable verification action: Inspect the raw tool observations, not just the final rationale. Require a direct statement about the same object and attribute—right-versus-left hemidiaphragm elevation. In this case, chest_xray_expert returned “Right” and llava_med_qa returned “the right hemidiaphragm appears to be elevated,” so the direct evidence supports “elevated right diaphragm.” Treat verify’s “CORRECT” as an audit of the proposed answer, not as independent image evidence. Also do not treat a projection word such as “lateral” as confirmed merely because it was inserted into the tool prompt or repeated in the rationale. Check for conflicting direct observations; if none, map the supported text to the displayed option and verify that the letter and text agree: A = “elevated right diaphragm,” matching the reference A. If direct observations conflict or the side is only echoed from a supplied phrase, obtain a neutral side check or record the side as unresolved rather than claiming consensus.

Lesson: In this case the terminal answer A, “elevated right diaphragm,” matched option A and the released reference A, “elevated right diaphragm,” so this was not an option-mapping error. The evidence also supported the conclusion: chest_xray_expert answered “Right” to the direct right-vs-left hemidiaphragm question, and maira2_grounded_report independently listed “Elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.” The final answer used that evidence. The reusable rule is to trace the supported side from a direct, non-leading observation and then map it back to the displayed option, rather than trusting the final letter or the rationale alone.

Narrow trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray answer whose alternatives differ only by laterality—for example, elevated right versus left diaphragm—after one or more visual tools have reported.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the letter, locate the tool result that directly answers the exact finding and side. Count as corroboration only a separate observation that states the same finding and side without being given that side as a prompt; do not count phrase grounding that merely boxes a supplied phrase, and do not count a report about a different attribute. If direct observations conflict, or if only an echoed/phrase-grounding result supports the side, treat the laterality as unresolved and obtain a neutral recheck rather than letting the final rationale select a side. Finally, map the supported finding text to the displayed options and confirm that the letter and text agree and match the reference-supported finding. In the supplied case, chest_xray_expert said “Right,” maira2_grounded_report independently said “Elevation of the right hemidiaphragm,” and option A was “elevated right diaphragm,” consistent with reference A.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest-X-ray multiple-choice answer that differs only by laterality (e.g., right vs left base pulmonary atelectasis) and the tool record contains one lateralized positive, one conflicting negative/indeterminate result, a view-specific “not applicable” result, and a verifier warning that laterality is not confirmable.

Verification action: Before emitting the option, reconcile each tool result against the exact object and attribute rather than counting positives. In this case, chest_xray_expert directly stated “Left base pulmonary atelectasis” (positive support); llava_med_qa stated no right/left base atelectasis (conflicting negative); maira2_grounded_report was not_applicable for a lateral-only image (not evidence); and verify returned PARTIALLY_CORRECT/CAUTION with laterality indeterminate (not confirmation). Do not use “expected answer” or “only positive finding among tools” as if it resolved the conflict. If lateralized evidence remains unresolved, do not describe the tools as consistent; either retain the ambiguity or rely only on the direct lateralized expert statement and note the limitation. Then map the supported text back to the displayed choice and verify letter/text agreement: B = “left base pulmonary atelectasis,” matching the reference B. This was not an option-mapping error; the reusable caution is that the final rationale overstated partial, conflicting evidence.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality (for example, elevated right versus left hemidiaphragm) after visual-QA tools have been consulted.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the option, read each cited tool observation and confirm it directly states the same finding and side—not merely “confirmed” or a phrase you supplied. Use only independent side-specific statements as evidence; a verifier’s “CORRECT” is not independent image evidence. Then map the supported finding text back to the displayed options and check that both letter and text agree. In this case, chest_xray_expert returned “Right” and llava_med_qa returned “the right hemidiaphragm appears to be elevated,” so the supported text matches A, “elevated right diaphragm” (reference A). If direct observations conflict or omit laterality, inspect the original image for projection/side marker, obtain a neutral side check, or record the side as unresolved rather than finalizing.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray answer whose choices differ only by laterality—right versus left—especially on a lateral view or when QA tools were asked a side-specific question.

Verification action: Before emitting the letter, separate “the finding is present” from “the finding is right-sided or left-sided.” Check whether any direct observation actually established laterality for the same object, such as an explicit side marker interpreted with anatomy or an orthogonal/frontal view. Do not count two QA models repeating the same side on the same lateral image as independent confirmation, because the hemithoraces overlap. Treat a verifier warning that the lateral view cannot reliably distinguish right from left as a conflict, and do not claim the side is confirmed by “two independent models.” Then map the supported finding text to the displayed option and check that the letter and text agree.

In this case the letter/text mapping was correct: A = “surgical instruments in the right lung,” matching the reference A. The lesson is about the evidence chain, not the option mapping: chest_xray_expert said “Right lung” and llava_med_qa also said “right hemithorax,” but verify warned that a single lateral view with only an L marker cannot reliably localize right versus left. The final rationale overstated the agreement as independent confirmation. The reusable procedure is to treat same-view repeated side answers as only weak laterality evidence, require an orthogonal view or explicit side/anatomical support before asserting right versus left, and still verify that the supported option letter and text match.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest-X-ray multiple-choice answer in which direct VQA/expert tools lateralize an opacity to one side, but a grounded-report tool returns a negative such as “lungs are free of focal infiltrates,” and the verifier labels the proposed option “CORRECT” while itself noting unresolved disagreement.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the final option, list each tool observation and classify it as independent positive evidence for the exact side/finding, negative presence evidence, or audit-only. Do not say “multiple tools consistently identify” unless the independent positives actually agree and the negative report has been addressed. Treat the verifier’s “CORRECT” as an audit of the proposed answer, not as an independent third positive; if the verifier says the conflict is unresolved, carry that uncertainty into the rationale or obtain another independent reader. In this case, chest_xray_expert and llava_med_qa directly said left lung opacity, while maira2_grounded_report said no focal infiltrates; the final reason should not have omitted that conflict while claiming verifier confirmation. Then map the supported answer text to the displayed choices and confirm letter and text agree: A = “left lung opacity,” which matches the reference, so the option mapping was correct but the evidence summary was overstated.

Trigger: When finalizing a multiple-choice chest X-ray answer whose options differ only by laterality—for example, A “left indwelling catheter” versus B “right indwelling catheter”—especially when the image is lateral, when VLM tools agree on a side, or when verify/reflect reports that laterality is ambiguous or not reliably determinable.

Verification action: Before emitting the final option, map the supported finding text back to the displayed choice and check that the letter and text agree. Then separate evidence: “catheter is present” proves presence only; “right” or “left” proves side only if it is an independent, neutral side-specific observation, not a phrase you supplied and not inferred from screen position. Treat a verifier statement such as “laterality is not reliably determinable” as direct uncertainty/conflict, not as “no evidence contradicts the side.” Do not let two VLM side guesses override that warning. Require independent side confirmation from a frontal/PA projection, side marker, or radiology report; if absent, record the side as unresolved rather than finalizing a confident side. The ROI crop limitation “Do not infer patient laterality from screen position” is an observable check here.

In this case, chest_xray_expert and llava_med_qa both said “right,” but verify reported that the catheter was visible while laterality was not reliably determinable on the lateral view, and roi_crop warned against inferring laterality from screen position. The terminal answer B “right indwelling catheter” was letter/text consistent, but it was an unsupported laterality conclusion, not a correct use of evidence; the reference was A “left indwelling catheter.” Earlier, verify was even called with “B. left indwelling catheter,” an option-text mismatch that should have been caught. The reusable lesson is that option mapping alone is insufficient: presence evidence and side evidence must be separated, and ambiguous laterality must not be converted into a confident side.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality (for example, right versus left indwelling catheter), especially on a lateral view or after using roi_crop to look for a side marker.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the option, require a direct, side-specific observation in the recorded evidence—a radiopaque “L” or “R” marker explicitly observed in the original image or crop, a frontal projection, or a radiology report. Treat roi_crop output as an inspection opportunity, not as proof that a marker exists; do not infer laterality from screen position or from a tool that merely confirms a catheter is present. In the source case, chest_xray_expert returned only “Yes,” llava_med_qa described a line but gave no side, and roi_crop returned only crop/box/image-path metadata—not an “L” marker. The terminal rationale’s “L marker” claim was therefore not supported by the recorded observations, even though B matched “left indwelling catheter” and the letter/text mapping was internally correct. Correct grade alone does not validate that evidence chain. If no independent side evidence is available, record laterality as unresolved or seek further confirmation; if it is available, map the supported finding text back to the displayed option and check that both letter and text agree.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality—such as left-base versus right-base atelectasis—and the image is a lateral/single view or tools give conflicting, ambiguous, or non-lateralizing responses.

Verification action: Before emitting the option, require each cited tool observation to explicitly state the same finding and the same patient side. Treat “Yes” to a combined “left or right?” question as non-lateralizing, “No” as no support, and a single model’s side-specific claim as a candidate only, not confirmation. Check whether the view can resolve laterality: on a lateral chest radiograph the bases are superimposed, so right-versus-left localization is not reliable without a frontal view, an explicit radiology report, or another independent side-specific source. Do not let “the only tool giving specific laterality” override direct negative or ambiguous evidence or a verifier caution. If laterality remains unverified, record it as indeterminate or seek the frontal view/report rather than finalizing a side. If a side is supported, then map the supported finding text to the displayed choice and verify that the letter and text agree.

In this case, B’s letter and text matched, so it was not an option-mapping error; the failure was using Medgemma’s right-side claim as sufficient while chest_xray_expert gave only “Yes” without a side, llava_med_qa said no, and the verifier explicitly warned that a lateral view could not confirm laterality. The reference was A, but the same evidence did not independently verify A either; the correct lesson is not to finalize a laterality that the available evidence cannot establish.

**Trigger:** When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by the laterality of a catheter (e.g., A "left indwelling catheter" vs. B "right indwelling catheter"), and the rationale cites a lateral-view side marker—such as an "L" next to the catheter hub—as proof of the catheter's side.

**Observable verification action:** Before emitting the option, confirm that the laterality evidence is catheter-specific, not merely the projection marker. On a lateral chest radiograph, the "L"/"R" marker denotes which side of the patient is positioned nearest the detector (the projection side); it does not by itself establish which side the catheter lies on. Treat only independent, side-specific statements about the catheter as laterality evidence, and check that they address the same object and attribute as the question. Separately, re-map every intermediate answer letter back to the displayed option list before finalizing, because an early letter/text mismatch can propagate.

**What went wrong in this case:** chest_xray_expert confirmed a catheter was present ("tip in the mid superior vena cava") but gave no side. llava_med_qa independently returned "right indwelling catheter" — the side that matched the released reference (B, right indwelling catheter). The verifier nevertheless read the lateral "L" marker as proving left-sided placement and recommended A (left). The terminal answer "A. left indwelling catheter" had consistent letter-and-text mapping, so this was not a terminal option-mapping error — it was a wrong laterality conclusion driven by over-reading the projection marker and discarding an independent side-specific observation.

There was, however, an intermediate mapping error worth flagging: the verify call was passed "B. left indwelling catheter" while the displayed map had A = left and B = right, i.e., a letter/text disagreement. Catching that before the verify step would have avoided feeding a broken mapping into the verifier.

**Reusable rule:** Do not convert a lateral-view side marker into catheter laterality. Verify what the marker actually labels (projection side), require catheter-specific side evidence, and confirm that each intermediate and final option's letter and text agree with the displayed map. Here the supported text ("right indwelling catheter") should have mapped to B, and the reference confirms B.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality—e.g., “small left pleural effusion” versus “small right pleural effusion”—and the image is a single lateral view while model/tool outputs name a side.

Verification action: Before emitting the choice, inspect each executed observation for a direct side statement about the same finding (pleural-effusion laterality) from a view or source capable of showing laterality, such as a frontal PA/AP view, decubitus view, ultrasound, or radiology report. Do not count two models both queried on the same lateral image as independent confirmation; a lateral marker “L” or “R” is an orientation/projection marker, not evidence of the effusion side. If no valid laterality evidence exists, treat the side as unresolved, or if forced-choice format requires a side, state the explicit consensus/non-visual basis rather than claiming independent image proof. Then map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and verify that its letter and text agree. In this case, B matched “small right pleural effusion” and the released reference B, so option mapping was correct; however, the final rationale overstated same-view model agreement as independent evidence and lost the verifier’s warning that a lateral-only image cannot reliably lateralize the effusion. This is a caution from the observed evidence failure, not proof that majority consensus on a lateral view is reliable.

Trigger: When finalizing a chest X-ray multiple-choice answer whose options differ only by laterality, such as A “right indwelling catheter” versus B “left indwelling catheter,” after side-specific visual-QA or report tools have been consulted.

Observable verification action: Before emitting the option, read each cited tool observation and require that it explicitly states the same finding and side, not merely that the finding is present and not merely coordinates or a box. For example, “Right side,” “right side,” and “right-sided central venous catheter” all directly support right laterality for the catheter. Treat “catheter present” alone, or a bounding box without an explicit side, as presence/localization evidence rather than side confirmation. If side-specific observations conflict or laterality is ambiguous, do not finalize a side without a neutral frontal-view/side-marker/report check. Then map the supported finding text to the displayed choices and confirm that the letter and text agree. In the supplied case, chest_xray_expert said “Right side,” llava_med_qa said “right side,” and maira2_grounded_report said “right-sided central venous catheter”; these addressed the same object and attribute, so A “right indwelling catheter” matched the supported evidence and the reference. The final rationale should not treat a box as proving the patient’s side unless the report itself names the side; here the report did name it.
